paper_title: What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Building on discrete diffusion models (Hoogeboom et al., 2021; Austin et al., 2021a; Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2024), masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Sakurai et al., 2026) provide an alternative to the left-toright generation of autoregressive models (Brown et al., 2020; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Qwen et al., Corresponding author. 1 2025) by iteratively refining partially masked sequences and committing multiple tokens in parallel. Their efficiency, however, depends strongly on the unmasking policy, which decides which positions to commit at each step. Conservative policies require many denoising evaluations, whereas unmasking many tokens at once can produce mutually inconsistent tokens, as they are predicted independently given the same state. Such errors persist, since committed tokens are not revised later (Wu et al., 2026; Jazbec et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Recent work therefore adapts the number of committed tokens to the decoding state. Training-free methods do so using confidence (Wu et al., 2026) or entropy-based dependence control (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), while learned policies are trained from data (Jazbec et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Despite this progress, learned unmasking policies differ in several design choices at once: which positions are labeled as safe to commit, which decoding states are used for training, and what information the policy observes, often together with policy capacity. For example, whether backbone hidden states help cannot be judged, since the policies that use them also differ in size or supervision. Prior work reports the number of function evaluations (NFE) and throughput, but the NFE reduction needed to offset policy overhead across policy sizes, caching, and prompt lengths remains unclear. We therefore revisit learned unmasking policies from distillation perspective. Existing supervised policies (Bao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) can be viewed as distilling fixed decoding procedure: the procedure is run on training prompts to obtain reference trajectories, teacher derived from them labels which positions may be committed, and the policy imitates this teacher. This view separates what the teacher labels, on which states the policy imitates it, and what the policy observes; we vary one at time, comparing choices from prior work with new candidates. First, existing teachers label prediction as committable whenever it matches the final output. correct token, however, is not necessarily safe to commit early, since its commitment changes the input to subsequent steps. We therefore introduce trajectory contraction, which labels commitment as valid only when it directly reaches later state of the reference trajectory, and compare it jointly with the choice of training states: reference trajectories or those induced by the labels. Second, as policy inputs, we compare confidence, probability margins, hidden representations, and confidence combined with hidden representations. Third, we measure both NFE and end-to-end throughput in tokens per second (TPS), and profile the policy overhead. Our study shows that matching the final output is an overly permissive label in the low-NFE regime, with 28.7% of such positives leaving the reference trajectory when committed early, and that hidden representations are weak alone but can complement confidence. It also shows that, across the tested settings, policy of up to 7.5M parameters pays off in throughput once it reduces NFE by more than about 10%. Based on these findings, we train policy with trajectory-contraction targets on reference trajectories, taking confidence and hidden representations as input; it has only 856K parameters, about 0.01% of the backbone. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025), our policy achieves the best accuracyNFE frontier on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), where it also attains the highest TPS at every accuracy target. On MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), it reaches moderate accuracy targets with the fewest NFE and the highest TPS, whereas training-free methods are more efficient at the highest targets, and on MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b) it performs comparably to the strongest baselines. Its advantage largely carries over to Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025) and, on mathematical reasoning, to unseen generation lengths. Our contributions are: We show that matching the final output is an overly permissive commitment label in the lowNFE regime, and introduce trajectory contraction, which improves the accuracyNFE frontier, with further out-of-domain gain from supervision on reference trajectories. We show that backbone hidden states alone are weak input, but can improve the frontier at high accuracy targets when combined with token confidence, and build on this an 856Kparameter policy. By profiling per-step latency, we show that policies of up to 7.5M parameters pay off in throughput once they reduce NFE by more than about 10% in the tested settings, and evaluate our policy across tasks, backbones, and generation lengths.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Efficient unmasking. The efficiency and quality of dLLMs depend strongly on the order and degree of parallelism used for unmasking (Kim et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Training-free approaches exploit predictive uncertainty, decoding dynamics, or dependencies among candidate positions to determine which tokens can be committed in parallel (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026; Luxembourg et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Fast-dLLM is particularly relevant to our setting: it uses confidence-thresholded parallel decoding to reduce denoising steps while keeping the underlying dLLM frozen (Wu et al., 2026). Despite substantial progress, these methods prescribe the commitment rule at inference time rather than learning it from decoding experience. Learning unmasking policies. Recent work instead learns where or when to commit tokens, using reinforcement learning, supervised oracle signals, ranking objectives, or learned dependency models (Hong et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Asano et al., 2026; Ringel et al., 2026). LUP learns lightweight Transformer policy from confidence-based features using reinforcement learning (Jazbec et al., 2026). More directly related to our supervision setting, Learn2PD trains lightweight filter from oracle token-correctness signals, whereas TraceLock derives commitment labels retrospectively from completed decoding traces and exploits richer hiddenstate representations (Bao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). We study how to construct supervised commitment targets directly from Fast-dLLM trajectories and how to incorporate richer token-level information without sacrificing the efficiency of lightweight confidence-based policies. 2 Method #Params Policy input Commitment target Training states Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026) LUP-conf (Jazbec et al., 2026) 2.1K confidence 7.5M 300K confidence hidden states LUP-hidden (Jazbec et al., 2026) 300M hidden states Candidates studied 331K856K c, h, [c, m], [c, h] terminal agreement terminal agreement reinforcement learning reinforcement learning terminal agreement, contraction teacher-induced reference on-policy rollouts on-policy rollouts reference, teacher-induced Table 1: Design choices of existing learned unmasking policies and the candidates compared in our study. sections.title: 3.2 Design Space and Protocol
sections.content: We study supervised policies trained offline on frozen backbone, such as Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026). These policies distill fixed decoding procedure: the procedure is run on training prompts to obtain reference trajectories, from which each masked position at each state is labeled with binary commitment target indicating whether it may be committed, and the policy is trained to predict these targets. Building such policy requires deciding what counts as correct commitment (the target), on which states the policy learns it (the training states; Section 3.3), and what the policy observes (the input; Section 3.4). Moreover, the policy is evaluated at every step, so its cost may offset the reduction in NFE (Section 3.5). Existing methods vary simultaneously across multiple design axes, making it difficult to isolate the effect of individual design choices from their reported results. For example, LUP-hidden 3 underperforms LUP-conf despite roughly 1000 more parameters (Jazbec et al., 2026)  (Table 1)  . We therefore compare existing and newly introduced candidates for each design axis while holding the others fixed. We evaluate the commitment target and training states jointly in 2 2 design to account for their interaction during teacher rollouts. Setup. We use LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) as the frozen backbone. Following Jazbec et al. (2026), all policies are trained on mixture of the GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) training sets, with reference trajectories generated by Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026) at confidence threshold 0.9. Unless otherwise specified, we use generation length = 256 and block length 32, and evaluate zero-shot. We take the accuracy of one-by-one confidencebased decoding (Nie et al., 2025) as the reference and define target accuracy levels at 98%, 95%, and 90% of it. For each method, we sweep its commitment threshold over fixed grid (Section C.4) and compare the resulting accuracyNFE trade-off against these targets. In this section, we evaluate on GSM8K (in-domain) and MBPP (out-of-domain) (Austin et al., 2021b), and all candidates share the same architecture, optimizer, and training schedule (Sections B.1 and C.3).

sections.content: Commitment targets. We consider two oracle criteria for defining supervision targets (Figure 1, panel (a)). Each oracle specifies which masked positions should be committed at given state. The first, terminal agreement, is used by both Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026). We compare the four combinations of two commitment targets (terminal agreement and trajectory contraction) and two training-state constructions (reference and teacher-induced trajectories), with the policy input fixed (Section B.1). As shown in Figure 2, replacing terminal agreement with trajectory contraction improves the frontier under both training-state constructions. On GSM8K, this change accounts for most of the gain, and both constructions perform comparably under contraction. On the out-of-domain MBPP, reference trajectories yield further improvement, reaching the 98% target with 48.6 NFE versus 64.8 for teacher4 dicts commitment score for each masked position. To isolate the effect of the input from policy capacity (Section 3.2), we keep the policy architecture fixed across configurations, varying only the input projection. Comparison. As shown in Figure 3, confidence provides strong low-dimensional signal, whereas hidden states alone require substantially more NFEs to reach the same accuracy on both tasks. Adding the margin yields no consistent gain. Combining confidence with hidden states reaches the 98% and 95% targets with the fewest NFE on both tasks, e.g., 42.1 versus 52.9 NFE for confidence alone at the 98% target on GSM8K. At the 90% target, however, confidence alone is comparable on GSM8K and slightly more efficient on MBPP. On MATH-500 and HumanEval, the benefit is less consistent, and adding the margin is competitive or better at the highest targets (Section B.6). These results suggest that hidden states can complement confidence; we hypothesize that their high dimensionality makes it difficult for lightweight policy to exploit them alone. This gain comes at cost: projecting the 4096-dimensional hidden state increases the policy from 331K to 856K parameters. Finding 2. Hidden representations underperform confidence when used alone but can complement it, mainly reducing the NFE needed to reach high accuracy targets; the gain varies across tasks.

sections.title: 3.5 Do NFE Gains Translate to Speedups?
sections.content: The comparisons above measure decoding efficiency by NFE. While NFE captures the number of backbone evaluations, it does not account for the computational overhead of the policy itself. This trade-off depends on policy size  (Table 1)  , including the 331K-to-856K increase from [c, h], and on backbone latency, which varies with prompt length and caching (Wu et al., 2026). We therefore profile per-step latency across these settings to determine how much NFE reduction is needed to improve throughput (Table 2; details in Section B.5). Besides our 331K and 856K policies, we include randomly initialized policies of 7.5M and 300M parameters, approximately matching TraceLock and LUP-hidden. The key result is that the break-even NFE reduction remains small for lightweight policies. Up to 7.5M parameters, the policy adds nearly constant cost of about 1.5 ms per step, at most 10% across Figure 3: AccuracyNFE frontiers for different inputs. induced trajectories. The gain from contraction is concentrated at low NFE; at the highest targets, terminal agreement can be more accurate (Section B.6). terminal agreement Two observations help interpret these results. First, is more permissive: 28.7% of its positive labels fall outside the contraction set (Section B.2). These are correct predictions that follow misprediction in the reference commitment order, so committing them early leads to state the reference trajectory never visits. Second, teacher-induced trajectories retain only 34% (contraction) and 25% (terminal agreement) of the reference states (Section B.3). This reduced coverage may explain why reference trajectories transfer better to MBPP, although it has little effect on GSM8K. Finding 1. Trajectory contraction yields better accuracyNFE frontier than terminal agreement, mainly in the low-NFE regime; training on reference trajectories gives further gain out of domain.

sections.title: 4 Putting the Findings Together
sections.content: We combine the findings into single policy, which we call OnTrack: Finding 1 determines its supervision (Section 4.2), Finding 2 its input (Section 4.1), and Finding 3 keeps its overhead small.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks and backbones. We follow the setup of Section 3.2 and extend the evaluation to MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), so that GSM8K and MATH-500 evaluate in-domain generalization and HumanEval and MBPP evaluate out-of-domain generalization to code. We additionally evaluate on Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025) (Section 5.4); implementation details are provided in Section C. Baselines. We compare against two training-free methods, Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026), which commits positions whose confidence exceeds threshold, and EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), which commits positions within an entropy budget, and against Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026), learned policy for which we use the official checkpoint. We do not include LUP (Jazbec et al., 2026) or TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026), as no trained checkpoints are publicly available for either method. Evaluation protocol. sections.title: 5.2 Main Results on LLaDA
sections.content: In-domain reasoning. On GSM8K, our policy yields the best frontier and reaches 98% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE (Figure 4, top). On MATH-500, it reaches the 95% target with the fewest NFE, but its accuracy saturates just below the 98% target, whereas EB-Sampler and Fast-dLLM exceed the reference at larger NFE. Out-of-domain code generation. Although the policy is trained only on mathematical reasoning, it transfers to code. On HumanEval, it reaches 90% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE, but Fast-dLLM is more efficient at the 95% target, and only Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler reach the 98% target. On MBPP, our policy reaches the 95% and 98% targets with the fewest NFE, whereas Learn2PD and Fast-dLLM are more efficient at the 90% target. Paired-bootstrap confidence intervals  (Table 27)  show that the NFE gains on GSM8K exceed evaluation noise against all baselines except EB-Sampler at the 98% target. Throughput. The NFE reductions carry over to throughput (Figure 4, bottom): at matched accuracy, our policy achieves the highest TPS on GSM8K across targets and on MATH-500 and HumanEval at moderate targets. On MBPP, it is close to the fastest baseline at the 95% and 98% targets but slower at the 90% target. Consistent with Finding 3, the 856K-parameter policys NFE advantage outweighs the overhead of evaluating it per step.

sections.title: 5.3 Compatibility with Prefix Caching
sections.content: We evaluate our policy and baselines with prefix caching (Wu et al., 2026) on GSM8K using zeroshot and four-shot prompts, following the latency analysis in Section 3.5. To ensure consistent accuracy targets across cached and uncached decoding, we use the uncached one-by-one baseline under the same prompting as the reference (78.0% zero-shot and 79.9% four-shot). Fewer NFE still means faster decoding. The reduction in NFE carries over to caching  (Table 3)  : with four-shot prompts, our policy remains the fastest at 98% of the reference accuracy. Despite the reduced backbone latency and increased relative policy overhead, its NFE advantage translates into higher throughput. Accuracy sensitivity. Caching reduces our policys accuracy by up to about two percentage points, while the baselines are less affected (Figure 10). With zero-shot prompts, Fast-dLLM overtakes our policy at the 98% accuracy target, although ours 7 Figure 5: Accuracy versus NFE on Dream-7B-Instruct. Dotted lines mark the reference accuracy and 98%, 95%, and 90% targets. Faded markers denote dominated operating points. Numerical results are in Tables 21 and 22.

sections.title: 5.5 Generalization Across Sequence Lengths
sections.content: We finally examine whether the learned policy generalizes across generation lengths without retraining. Following the length-transfer setting of Jazbec et al. (2026), we train the policy with = 256 and evaluate the same checkpoint at = 128 and = 512 on GSM8K and MATH-500, keeping the block length fixed at 32. As shown in Figure 6, the policy largely retains its advantage under both length shifts: it yields the best or comparable frontier up to 95% of the reference accuracy at both lengths, and at = 128 it reaches 98% on MATH-500 with the fewest NFE. At = 512, it saturates below 98% on MATH500, where Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler exceed the reference at larger NFE. When the length shift is combined with the domain shift to code, however, the policy falls behind Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler on HumanEval and MBPP (Section C.6), indicating that it tolerates either shift alone but not both.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We revisited learned unmasking policies for dLLMs through controlled study of supervision, inputs, and overhead. Trajectory-contraction targets improve the accuracyNFE frontier mainly at low NFE, with further out-of-domain gain from reference trajectories. Hidden representations are weak alone but can complement confidence at high accuracy targets. Policies of up to 7.5M parameters pay off in throughput once they reduce NFE by more than about 10% in the tested settings. Building on these findings, our 856K-parameter policy reaches moderate accuracy targets with the best or comparable efficiency across two backbones, transfers from mathematical reasoning to code, and converts its NFE reductions into throughput gains. Figure 6: Accuracy-NFE trade-off at = 128 (top) and = 512 (bottom), using policy trained at = 256. Results on HumanEval and MBPP are provided in Section C.6; numerical results in Tables 23 and 25. remains the fastest at 95% (Table 3; see Section 7).

sections.title: 5.4 Generalization Across Backbones
sections.content: We next examine whether our design transfers to different dLLM. We apply the same procedure to Dream-7B-Instruct, training separate policy with the same training data, trajectory-contraction supervision, and policy-training procedure. Since Dream has hidden dimension of 3584, the policy has 790K parameters. Figure 5 shows that the advantage of our policy is largely preserved. It yields the best frontier on HumanEval, where it exceeds the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE, and reaches 98% of the reference accuracy on MATH-500 with the fewest NFE. On GSM8K, it reaches 95% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE but saturates slightly below the reference, where Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler are more accurate at larger NFE. On MBPP, all methods reach the targets within narrow NFE range and perform comparably. 8 et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b)) and models (LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025)) are publicly available and used in accordance with their licenses. Our implementation builds on the publicly released codebase of Learning Unmasking Policies for Diffusion Language Models (Jazbec et al., 2026), with modifications for our proposed policy training and decoding methods. We collect no new data involving human subjects. Use of AI assistants. We used AI assistants to support code development, figure preparation, and language polishing of the manuscript. sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: Training and evaluation scope. Our policy is trained only on mathematical reasoning data at single generation length (L = 256) with fixed block length. It transfers to code at the training length and to other lengths on mathematical tasks, but its advantage does not persist when both shifts occur together (Section 5.5). Training on multiple domains and generation lengths is natural remedy that we leave to future work. High-accuracy regime. On some tasks (MATH500 on LLaDA and GSM8K on Dream), the accuracy of our policy saturates slightly below the reference, even with conservative thresholds, whereas training-free methods reach the reference at larger NFE. Our policy is therefore most beneficial at moderate accuracy targets, and closing this gap may require supervision that covers more conservative commitment behavior. Sensitivity to backbone features. Approximate inference such as prefix caching reduces the accuracy of our policy by up to about two points, whereas confidence-based baselines are essentially unaffected (Section 5.3). The drop persists even when the policy unmasks one token per step, so it concerns which tokens are committed rather than how many. plausible cause is that the policy consumes backbone hidden representations, which caching perturbs; making learned unmasking policies robust to approximate inference is left to future work.

sections.title: 8 Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Environmental impact. This work aims to reduce the computational cost of inference with diffusion language models, potentially lowering energy consumption. However, the overall environmental impact depends on deployment scale, as improved efficiency may encourage greater model usage. Potential risks. Faster inference may facilitate large-scale generation of misleading or harmful content. Our method does not modify backbone parameters and only determines when to commit the backbones predictions. It therefore inherits the capabilities, biases, and failure modes of the underlying models. Changes in decoding may also affect output safety, which we do not explicitly evaluate. sections.title: B Controlled Study Details
sections.content: B.1 Experimental Setup Controlled experiments follow the training and decoding configuration in Sections C.2 and C.3 and are evaluated on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b). The reference accuracy is that of one-by-one confidence-based decoding (78.0% on GSM8K, 38.8% on MATH-500, 45.1% on HumanEval, and 52.9% on MBPP), and 13 the accuracy targets are 98%, 95%, and 90% of it. For each policy, we sweep the commitment threshold γ over the grid in Table 12 and report the frontier of non-dominated operating points. Each comparison varies single factor while keeping the others fixed, as summarized in Table 5. Section Varied Section 3.3 Section 3.4 label, training states policy input Fixed input [c, h] contraction, reference Table 5: Factors varied and fixed in the controlled comparisons. All other settings follow Section C.3. B.2 Commitment Target Construction Trajectory-contraction targets are constructed as described in Section A.2. Terminal agreement. We use the final token of the reference trajectory, generated by Fast-dLLM with threshold 0.9, as the terminal target . This corresponds to the labeling rule shared by Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026), which label prediction by its agreement with the terminal output of fixed decoding procedure. For teacher-induced trajectories, the same is used even after the trajectory departs from the reference. Agreementcontraction mismatch. Since valid contraction commits only tokens that match the reference trajectory, contraction positives are always subset of terminal-agreement positives. Over all reference trajectories, 28.7% of terminalagreement positives violate trajectory contraction, i.e., they are correct tokens whose commitment at st would leave the reference trajectory, and 56.0% of reference states contain at least one such violation. The fraction is consistent across datasets (28.5% on GSM8K and 29.1% on MATH). B.3 Training-Trajectory Construction Reference trajectories. Targets are computed on every state of the reference trajectory, and the policy is trained on all of these states. Teacher-induced trajectories. Starting from s0, we repeatedly apply the teacher, committing every positively labeled position, and train on the resulting states. Under trajectory contraction, the teacher jumps from st to su , so the induced trajectory is subsequence of the reference trajectory and its targets are inherited from it. Under terminal agreement, the induced states generally leave the reference trajectory; we therefore run the backbone on each induced state to obtain new predictions and recompute targets. Table 6 reports the number of training states under each configuration. Teacherinduced trajectories retain only fraction of the reference states: 34.0% under trajectory contraction and 25.4% under terminal agreement. The hidden repreR4096 is taken from the final layer sentation ht,i of the backbone. Each input is linearly projected to = 128 dimensions before entering the shared policy network fϕ. They are obtained by profiling LLaDA-8B-Instruct on single H200 GPU with batch size 1, generation length = 256, block length 32, and commitment threshold 0.9, using synthetic prompts of 128 to 2048 tokens. Within each row, the backbone latency is the median over all policy configurations, so differences across columns reflect only the policy and bookkeeping. Policy sizes. The 331K and 856K columns are the trained Conf. and Conf.+Hidden policies used in our experiments. To see how the overhead grows with policy size, we add two larger policies whose parameter counts roughly match those of policies in prior work: the 7.5M policy is about the size of the TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026) network, and the 300M policy is about the size of the LUP-hidden (Jazbec et al., 2026) network. These two policies do not reproduce the architectures of those methods. Both are scaled-up versions of our Conf.+Hidden policy, with widths chosen to approximately match the target parameter counts. The 7.5M policy uses hidden width 512, feed-forward width 2400, and 8 attention heads, with one block in each of the confidence and hidden streams (7.52M parameters). The 300M policy uses hidden width 2048, feed-forward width 7296, and 16 heads, with four blocks in each stream (300.3M parameters). Both policies are randomly initialized and are used only for latency measurement. This does not bias the measurement, because the cost of policy forward pass depends on its architecture and input shape, not on its weights, and the per-step latency is measured independently of the decisions the policy makes. 14 Dataset GSM8K MATH MATH-500 HumanEval MBPP Total Training Evaluation 7,473 7,485 14, 1,319 500 164 257 2,240 Table 9: Training and evaluation dataset sizes. 98% with the fewest NFE and the highest accuracy, exceeding the reference. sections.title: C Experimental Details
sections.content: C.1 Datasets and Prompt Templates Datasets. We train on the GSM8K training split (openai/gsm8k) and the MATH training split (ankner/math-500). For MATH, we exclude 15 examples whose gold answers cannot be parsed by the answer verifier, leaving 7,485 examples. The resulting 14,958 training examples are concatenated and shuffled with seed 42. During training, prompts exceeding 256 tokens are left-truncated to retain the last 256 tokens. Evaluation prompts are not truncated, and no evaluation examples are used for training. Table 9 summarizes the dataset sizes. All evaluations use zero-shot prompting unless otherwise stated. GSM8K uses the openai/gsm8k test split, MATH-500 uses HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500, HumanEval uses openai/openai_humaneval, and MBPP uses the sanitized test split of google-research-datasets/mbpp. Prompt templates. We use task-specific instruction prompts with the backbones chat template. For GSM8K and MATH, we use the same prompt for training and evaluation, instructing the model to solve problems step by step and provide the final answer in boxed{}. For HumanEval and MBPP, we follow the prompts from lm-eval. HumanEval provides function signature and docstring, while MBPP provides task description and test cases. For both tasks, generation continues from partially provided code block. Answer verification. For GSM8K and MATH, we extract and verify the final boxed answer using math-verify v0.8.0. The same procedure is used Figure 8: AccuracyNFE frontiers for the 2 2 supervision designs on MATH-500 and HumanEval. Faded markers denote dominated operating points. Figure 9: AccuracyNFE frontiers for different policy inputs on MATH-500 and HumanEval. Faded markers denote dominated operating points. B.6 Results on MATH-500 and HumanEval Figures 8 and 9 repeat the comparisons of Sections 3.3 and 3.4 on MATH-500 and HumanEval, with the same configurations  (Table 5)  . Supervision. On HumanEval, combining trajectory contraction with reference trajectories yields the best frontier throughout, reaches the 90% target with the fewest NFE, and is the only configuration to reach the 95% target, whereas terminal agreement on reference trajectories remains below 90% at all operating points. On MATH-500, the same combination yields the best frontier up to the 95% target but saturates just below 98%, whereas the other configurations reach 98% at larger NFE, with terminal agreement on reference trajectories exceeding the reference accuracy. Trajectory contraction thus mainly improves the low-NFE regime, consistent with Finding 1. Policy input. Hidden states alone remain below 95% of the reference accuracy on MATH-500 and below 90% on HumanEval. C.2 Policy Optimization We train the full policy jointly with AdamW. Training takes approximately 3 hours and 15 minutes on single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Unless otherwise specified, all policy-training experiments use the hyperparameters in Table 10. C.3 Training and Decoding Configuration Following Jazbec et al. (2026), we train the policy on the training splits of GSM8K and MATH. We retain only reference trajectories whose final answer is correct, yielding 9,169 trajectories. No codegeneration examples are used for policy training; HumanEval and MBPP therefore evaluate out-ofdomain generalization from mathematical reasoning to code. Reference trajectories are generated by FastdLLM (Wu et al., 2026) with confidence threshold of 0.9. We use generation length = 256 and block length 32 for both trajectory collection and the main evaluation. For the length-transfer evaluation at = 512 (Section 5.5), we additionally apply End-of-Text Prediction (EoTP) (Bao et al., 2026) to all methods: once an end-of-text token has been committed, all remaining masked positions after it are filled with end-of-text tokens, and decoding terminates. As result, the NFE at = 512 can be smaller than even for one-by-one decoding. The trajectory-generation temperature is set to zero. The frozen LLaDA-8B-Instruct backbone is loaded in bfloat16, while policy computation is performed in float32. The backbone parameters remain frozen throughout policy training.
